title: The Domestic Cat
imageAlt: An African wildcat crouched in the shade of a green desert shrub, looking back through the leaves with its ears lit orange by low sun; its sandy, faintly striped coat is almost indistinguishable from a domestic tabby's.
summary: There is no good reason for the cat to exist. Every other animal we domesticated had a job — pulling, carrying, laying, being eaten — and the work reshaped it until it barely resembled its wild ancestor. The cat took no job and barely changed: stand a house cat beside the African wildcat it descends from and only an expert can tell them apart. For a century the explanation was that cats invited themselves into the first farming villages to eat the mice in the grain, and stayed. In November 2025 a study of ancient genomes took that apart, and the replacement is stranger: the cat may owe its existence to an Egyptian religious industry that bred it in the millions to kill it.

The old story rested on two things. One was a grave dug 9,500 years ago at Shillourokambos in southern Cyprus, published in 2004 by the archaeologist Jean-Denis Vigne: a human buried with ochre, seashells and flint tools, and forty centimetres away a cat of about eight months. Cats are not native to Cyprus, so somebody had carried this one across open sea. The other was mitochondrial DNA — the scrap of genetic code passed down the maternal line — which seemed to show cats reaching Europe from Anatolia with Neolithic farmers 6,000 years ago.

Mitochondrial DNA was the weak link. On 27 November 2025 a team led by Marco De Martino and Claudio Ottoni published a paper in Science reading the far larger nuclear genome of seventy ancient cats. Almost every supposed early domestic cat in Europe dissolved on inspection: they were European wildcats, carrying a trace of African ancestry from old interbreeding, enough to fool a maternal-line test. The Cyprus cat now looks like a tamed wild animal, and true domestic cats, descended from the North African wildcat, do not reach Europe until about two thousand years ago.

Which puts Egypt at the centre of it. Cats there were bound up with Bastet, a goddess shown first as a lioness, later as a seated house cat. What her worshippers bought was an offering, and the offering was a mummified cat; millions were made. X-rays show most died violently, of a broken neck or a crushed skull; archaeologists think temples ran catteries to meet demand. Sean Doherty, a zooarchaeologist at Exeter, argues that domestication happened here: breeding cats by the million, and selecting without meaning to for animals that were easy to handle. His paper is still a preprint and contested, but it fits the dates better than the granary does.

However it began, the spread was Roman. Domestic cats move out of North Africa along military and trade routes, fast, reaching Britain by the first century AD, travelling the way rats travelled — in the holds of ships. The evidence is often accidental: archaeologists ahead of the Lincoln bypass in 2016 found a Roman roof tile with a cat's pawprint pressed into it while the clay dried in the sun. Dog prints on Roman tiles are common; cat prints are rare — about what you would expect of a new arrival.

Medieval Europe was harder on cats, though not as hard as the internet insists. The story that a papal letter of 1233 set off a continent-wide cat cull, letting the rats bring the Black Death, is not in the document, which went to one archbishop, concerns a heretical cult in the Rhineland and tells nobody to kill anything. Cats were killed in Europe, at festivals and in witch trials, but the great extermination is a modern invention. The period did change the cats. The blotched tabby, the swirled marbling most tabbies wear now, does not appear until the Middle Ages; before that, essentially every cat was striped like a wildcat. Somebody had started choosing cats for their looks.

That instinct was formalised in July 1871, when the illustrator Harrison Weir talked the Crystal Palace Company into staging an Exhibition of Cats. Around a hundred and seventy animals were judged against standards Weir had written himself — the first time anyone had set down what a good cat should look like. His motive was reform rather than snobbery: he wanted people to stop kicking cats. Within twenty years there were pedigrees, a National Cat Club and the beginnings of the breeds we have now.

The cat became an indoor animal much later, and for an odd reason. Until the 1940s an indoor cat meant a box of ash or sawdust and a house that smelled of it, so cats were put out at night. In January 1947 a neighbour, Kay Draper, asked Ed Lowe of Cassopolis, Michigan, for sand: her cat's box had frozen solid. Lowe's family sold industrial absorbents, so he gave her granulated clay instead. She came back for more. He filled ten five-pound bags, wrote “Kitty Litter” on them and asked sixty-five cents each, when sand cost a penny a pound. Shops thought he was mad, so he told them to give it away; customers came back with money. By the mid-1980s American homes held more cats than dogs.

The bill is paid somewhere else. Free-ranging cats — pets that go out, and the far larger population belonging to nobody — are among the most destructive introduced predators alive. A 2016 analysis in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences implicated cats in 63 known extinctions of birds, mammals and reptiles — a quarter of all recorded extinctions in those groups. In the United States alone they are thought to kill between 1.3 and 4 billion birds a year. And the animal doing it is still only half-tamed, interbreeding with wildcats so freely that the European wildcat is being absorbed into it. We have had the cat for between two and ten thousand years, depending which paper you read this month, and we still do not know why.

didYouKnow.text: In February 1890 a ship docked at Liverpool carrying roughly 180,000 mummified Egyptian cats — about nineteen and a half tons of them — dug out of the catacombs at Istabl Antar, near Beni Hasan, where they had been left as offerings to the lioness goddess Pakhet. They were auctioned on 10 February and spread on English fields as fertiliser. A handful were rescued and given to the museum in Liverpool, which still has one.

momentFromHistory.title: A first-class carriage to the first cat show
momentFromHistory.text: In July 1871 Harrison Weir took the train from Ludgate Hill out to the Crystal Palace, to judge a competition he had invented and was not at all sure would work. “Sitting alone in the comfortable cushioned compartment of a ‘first class,’” he wrote, “I confess I felt somewhat more than anxious as to the issue of the experiment. Yes; what would it be like? Would there be many cats? How many?” A friend got in along the way, heard where he was going, said he hated cats and drove them off his own property, and predicted a great deal of clutching at bars and strangling on chains. Inside the Palace they found the opposite: the cats lay in their pens on crimson cushions lapping new milk, “making no sound save now and then a homely purring”. Weir called on the same friend a few months later and found him at lunch with two cats on the chair beside him.
